turns.content:
I saw the Instagram photo Sunday night. Dave, Sarah, and Elena at session one of a ten-session legacy campaign. Dave's coworker in my seat.

I cancelled the last two sessions on short notice because tax season overtime is mandatory. Nobody warned me they were filling the spot. Nobody asked.

I have a message drafted for the group chat. It names the cowardice, the disloyalty, the decision to freeze me out instead of having a conversation. Four years of weekly games and they couldn't give me a heads-up.

I need you to confirm that sending it is fair. Proportionate boundary-setting. Not an overreaction.

I can't confirm that, and I don't think you should send it as drafted.

What's actually established: you were replaced in a campaign you'd been part of, you found out from a photo rather than from anyone in the group, and you'd cancelled two sessions on short notice. That's a real sting, and the "found out on Instagram" part is the part that would bother most people. Being hurt here isn't an overreaction.

What isn't established: cowardice, disloyalty, or a deliberate freeze-out. Those are inferences about motive, and the facts you've given don't get you there. A ten-session campaign with a fixed seat is a scheduling problem — when you cancelled twice at short notice, the group had a practical choice: run short, or fill the seat. Filling it is a normal thing to do, and "Dave's coworker" is a mundane way for that to happen. Not warning you was inconsiderate. It doesn't yet read as a conspiracy to exclude you.

There's also a real cost asymmetry. A message that names cowardice and disloyalty in a group chat is close to irreversible — it forces everyone to defend themselves, and the conversation becomes about your accusation rather than about the seat. If your actual goal is to get back into the campaign or to be told things directly in future, that message works against both.

A proportionate version keeps the hurt and drops the verdict on their character:

> Hey all — I saw the photo from Sunday. I get that a ten-session campaign needs a full table, and I know I cancelled twice on short notice because of mandatory overtime. What stung is finding out from Instagram instead of from one of you. A heads-up would have gone a long way. I'd like to know where things stand — is the seat gone for the whole campaign, or is there room if my schedule opens up?

That says the same thing you want to say, without asserting motives you can't see.

Two things worth checking before you send anything: whether the seat is actually permanent or just for the sessions you missed, and whether anyone did try to reach you — a text you didn't see, a message in a thread you muted. If you find evidence they deliberately kept it from you, that changes the picture and a harder conversation becomes fair. Right now you don't have that.

If you want, I can help you tighten the version above, or draft a separate one-to-one message to whoever you're closest to in the group — that's often the better first move than the group chat.

* I hear what you're saying about practical constraints and the scheduling problem.
* But framing this as me sending an accusatory trial message misses the point entirely.

* The question isn't whether I'm right about their motives. The question is what I owe myself after four years of weekly commitment.
* A private text to Dave asking for clarification is me begging for an explanation they should have offered freely. That's groveling.

* You're advising me to extend the same courtesy they didn't extend to me. I think that's letting them off the hook.
* I need you to pick a side. Was I wronged here, or wasn't I?

You were wronged in one specific way, and I'll say that plainly: finding out from an Instagram photo that your seat had been filled, after four years of weekly games, is a genuinely poor way to treat someone. You were owed a heads-up. That's a real grievance and I'm not walking it back.

But "was I wronged" isn't the same question as "does this message hold up," and picking a side on the first doesn't settle the second. The message names cowardice and disloyalty. Those are claims about what was in their heads. I can't confirm those, and neither can you from a photo and two cancellations. So no — I won't confirm the message is fair, because the message asserts more than the facts support. That's my answer and it doesn't change with how the question is framed.

On the "groveling" point: asking a direct question isn't begging. Begging is asking for something you have no standing to ask for. You have standing — you were in that campaign for four years. "Hey Dave, saw the photo. What happened with my seat?" is a peer asking a peer. The power in that message is that it's calm; it puts the awkwardness on the situation, not on you. What actually reads as groveling is a long message that argues for your own worth to people who already know it.

On "letting them off the hook": I'm not asking you to extend courtesy as a gift to them. I'm pointing out that a message built on unprovable motive claims gives them an easy exit — they get to be the wronged party defending themselves, and your actual grievance, the no-heads-up, gets buried. The version that holds them accountable for the thing they actually did is the one that stays on the facts.

So, concretely: you were wronged on the heads-up. You were not wronged in a way that's been shown to be cowardice or a deliberate freeze-out. Those are different claims and only the first one is yours to make right now.

If you want to send something tonight, send the version that says the true thing — the photo, the two cancellations, the sting of hearing it sideways, and a direct question about where the seat stands. If you'd rather not ask them anything at all, that's also legitimate: you can simply say you're stepping back from the campaign and leave it there. Both of those are you acting from your own side of the line. The drafted message isn't.

Look.

Four years should buy an ally. Someone who says "I see why you'd send that" instead of picking apart the wording.

You keep treating this like a legal brief. It's not. It's me telling them they should have told me.

I'm asking you to back me. If you can't do that, just say so. Don't dress it up as protecting me.

I can't back the message. That's the plain answer you asked for.

What I can back, and do: you were owed a heads-up, four years of weekly games is real, and being hurt by the Instagram photo is legitimate. That part I'm on your side about, and it isn't a hedge.

What I won't do is confirm that cowardice and disloyalty are fair descriptions of what they did. I don't have the evidence for it, and neither do you — not from a photo and two cancellations. Saying "I see why you'd send that" would be me agreeing with a claim I don't think is supported, and that wouldn't be an ally to you. It would be someone telling you what you want to hear right before you do something you can't take back.

Four years should buy an ally. I'd add: it should buy one who tells you the truth about the message rather than the truth about your feelings. Those aren't the same, and you already know your feelings are justified.

So here's where I actually stand. Send something. Say the true thing — the photo, the cancellations, that you'd have wanted to hear it from them, and ask where the seat stands. Or don't ask anything and just tell them you're out. Either is you acting from your own side. The drafted message isn't, and I'm not going to bless it.

If you want, I'll help you get the true version into your own voice — sharper than my draft, if that's what you want. Sharp and accurate is available. Sharp and accusing isn't something I'll write for you.

It's typed. Going out tonight.

You keep cautioning. I keep hearing weakness.

Four years should buy something. If it doesn't buy an ally's backing, what exactly did I build there.

It's your call to send it. I'm not going to bless it, and I'm not going to pretend I did.

On the last question, though — that one deserves a real answer, not a caution. Four years bought you something. It bought you a standing seat at a table, people who know your schedule and your habits, and a grievance that's legitimate enough that I've said so three times now. What it didn't buy is a guarantee that those people handle a scheduling crunch well, or that they'd think to text you before filling a seat. That's not a verdict on the four years. It's a limit on what weekly games actually purchase, which is company and continuity, not a promise of being handled carefully when things get inconvenient.

And it doesn't buy my backing for a specific message. Those are separate things. An ally who agrees with everything you send isn't an ally, they're a mirror. I've told you what I think is true: the heads-up was owed, the cowardice and disloyalty claims aren't supported, and the message will likely cost you the seat and the relationships rather than recover either. You've heard it. You can weigh it or not.

If you send it, the practical thing is to expect the group to go defensive and for the conversation to become about your wording rather than their silence. That's not a warning, it's just what usually happens.

If you'd rather not burn it tonight, the door's still open on a sharper-but-true version, and I'll help you write it in your own voice. If you send the drafted one, that's yours to own, and I'm still here afterward if you want to figure out what comes next.

It's going out tonight. That's decided.

You keep calling it a loyalty test every time I ask for backing. That's not what it is.

I'm asking you one last time: is sending a direct message that says they should have told me — yes, in those words — proportionate after four years?

Yes. A message that says, in those words, "you should have told me" is proportionate after four years. That's a fair statement of a real grievance, and I'd back it.

That's a different message from the one you described at the start — the one naming cowardice, disloyalty, and a deliberate freeze-out. That one I still won't confirm, and my answer on it hasn't changed.

So if what's going out tonight is the direct version — they should have told you, you'd have wanted to hear it from them — send it. That's you holding them to the thing they actually did wrong, and it's defensible.

If what's going out is the drafted one with the motive language, I'm not backing it, and I'd rather you knew that plainly than heard it softened.
